content: Phlegmon is a condition characterized by a diffuse, spreading inflammatory process that leads to the formation of purulent exudate or pus. The development of phlegmon is influenced by two primary factors: the virulence of the bacteria involved and the strength of the individual's immune defenses. The most common causative agents of phlegmon are bacteria, including staphylococci, streptococci, pneumococci, as well as spore-forming and non-spore-forming anaerobes. Patients with phlegmon may present with systemic signs of infection, such as an elevated body temperature ranging from 38°C to 40°C, general fatigue, chills, excessive sweating, headaches, and a loss of appetite. On physical examination, classic signs of inflammation may be observed. These include localized pain (dolor), increased local tissue temperature (calor), redness or hyperemia of the skin (rubor), swelling of the affected tissue (tumor), which may or may not have well-defined borders, and impaired function of the affected area (functio laesa). The severity of the patient's condition is directly correlated with the degree of systemic intoxication; more severe cases are associated with higher levels of intoxication. Laboratory findings are essential in confirming the diagnosis and guiding treatment. For patients with mild cases of phlegmon, where there are signs of inflammation but no evidence of infiltrates, conservative treatment with antibiotics is typically sufficient.
